kcet|Chemistry|2009|2||0|0:
Potassium has Z = 19, so its configuration is
K = 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ **4s¹**
The 4s orbital fills before 3d because of the (n + l) rule: 4s has n + l = 4 + 0 = 4, while 3d has
3 + 2 = 5, so 4s is lower in energy.
The outermost electron is therefore the lone 4s electron. Read off its quantum numbers:
n = 4 — the fourth shell
l = 0 — an s orbital
m = 0 — an s orbital is spherical, so there is only one orientation and m can only be 0
s = +½ — the convention for a single unpaired electron
Options (2) and (4) give n = 3, which would put the electron in the third shell, and (3) gives
l = 1, which would make it a p electron. Neither matches 4s¹.
∴ 4, 0, 0, +½.

kcet|Chemistry|2009|7||0|0.s:
The compound must contain all three kinds of linkage at once, so look for an ion that is
itself held together by a coordinate bond.
NH₄Cl does exactly that.
**Covalent** — in the ammonia part, nitrogen shares an electron pair with each of three
hydrogens: three N–H covalent bonds.
**Coordinate** — the fourth hydrogen arrives as a bare proton, H⁺, with no electrons of its own.
Nitrogen's lone pair supplies **both** electrons for that bond, making it coordinate (dative).
**Ionic** — the resulting NH₄⁺ is then held to Cl⁻ by electrostatic attraction.
So all three appear in one formula unit.
The others fall short: NaCl and CaO are purely ionic, and NH₃ has only covalent bonds — its
lone pair is still unused.
(Note that once formed, all four N–H bonds in NH₄⁺ are identical and indistinguishable; the
distinction is about how the bond was made.)
∴ NH₄Cl.

kcet|Chemistry|2009|8||0|0:
A pyramidal AB₃ molecule is ammonia-like, so work from VSEPR.
For the shape to be pyramidal rather than trigonal planar, the central atom must carry a lone
pair that pushes the three bonds downwards.
That means four electron domains in total:
3 bond pairs, one to each B atom
1 lone pair on A
The four domains take up a tetrahedral arrangement, and with one position occupied by the
lone pair the three atoms form a pyramid — the lone pair repels more strongly than a bond
pair, so the angle closes slightly below 109°28′ (107° in NH₃).
Had there been no lone pair, the four would have been three bond pairs only, giving a flat
trigonal planar shape as in BF₃ — which is option (4) and the usual wrong answer.
∴ 1 lone pair and 3 bond pairs.

kcet|Chemistry|2009|9||0|0.s:
Follow the calcium through, since none of it is lost.
moles of Ca(OH)₂ = 0.050 L × 0.5 mol L⁻¹ = 0.025 mol
Excess CO₂ first converts the hydroxide to the soluble hydrogencarbonate:
Ca(OH)₂ + 2CO₂ ⇒ Ca(HCO₃)₂
but evaporating to dryness decomposes that back again:
Ca(HCO₃)₂ ⇒ CaCO₃ + H₂O + CO₂
So the solid is 0.025 mol of CaCO₃.
Neutralising it takes two moles of acid per mole of carbonate:
CaCO₃ + 2HCl ⇒ CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂
equivalents of CaCO₃ = 0.025 × 2 = 0.05
volume of 0.1 N HCl = 0.05 / 0.1 = 0.5 L = 500 cm³
Forgetting the factor of 2 gives 250 cm³; the carbonate is dibasic, which is what the use of
**normality** in the question is signalling.
∴ 500 cm³.

kcet|Chemistry|2009|10||0|0.s:
Equivalent mass and atomic mass are related through the valency:
atomic mass = equivalent mass × valency
The metal is bivalent, so
atomic mass = 32 × 2 = 64
(That identifies it as copper, though the name is not needed.)
A bivalent metal forms the nitrate M(NO₃)₂. The nitrate group NO₃ has mass
14 + 3(16) = 62
so the formula mass is
64 + 2 × 62 = 64 + 124 = 188
Option (1), 192, comes from using 64 with an incorrectly rounded nitrate mass, and (4), 168,
from taking the metal as monovalent.
∴ 188.

kcet|Chemistry|2009|11||0|0.s:
The root mean square speed can be written in terms of pressure and density, which is exactly
what is given here:
u(rms) = √(3P/d)
This form comes from pV = ⅓mNu², since density d = mN/V.
Substitute P = 1.2 × 10⁵ N m⁻² and d = 4 kg m⁻³:
u = √(3 × 1.2 × 10⁵ / 4)
= √(3.6 × 10⁵ / 4)
= √(9 × 10⁴)
= 300 m s⁻¹
The numbers are chosen to give a perfect square, which is a useful check that the right form
of the equation has been used.
Note the alternative form u = √(3RT/M) cannot be used here, since neither temperature nor
molar mass is given.
∴ 300 m s⁻¹.

kcet|Chemistry|2009|12||0|0.s:
A hole in the container means the gases **effuse** out, and Graham's law governs the rates:
rate ∝ 1/√M
So the lightest gas escapes fastest and is depleted most; the heaviest escapes slowest and is
left behind.
Molar masses:
H₂ = 2 — lightest, effuses fastest, so least of it remains
CH₄ = 16 — intermediate
SO₂ = 64 — heaviest, effuses slowest, so most of it remains
Relative rates are √(64/2) ≈ 5.7 times faster for H₂ than SO₂, so after three hours the
difference is substantial.
Partial pressure is proportional to the moles remaining, so the order of partial pressures is
the reverse of the order of effusion rates:
pSO₂ > pCH₄ > pH₂
They started equal at 0.5 mol each, so this ordering is entirely the work of the hole.
∴ pSO₂ > pCH₄ > pH₂.

kcet|Chemistry|2009|13||0|0:
The enthalpy of formation refers to making **one mole** of the compound from its elements:
½N₂(g) + 3/2H₂(g) ⇒ NH₃(g), ΔH = −46 kJ mol⁻¹
The reaction asked about is the decomposition of **two** moles, so it is the formation reaction
reversed and doubled.
Reverse it — change the sign:
NH₃ ⇒ ½N₂ + 3/2H₂, ΔH = +46 kJ
Double it — double the value:
2NH₃(g) ⇒ N₂(g) + 3H₂(g), ΔH = +92 kJ
Both operations are needed, and each is a place a mark is commonly lost: forgetting the sign
gives −92, and forgetting to double gives +46.
The positive sign makes sense — ammonia is stable, so energy must be supplied to break it up.
∴ +92 kJ.
kcet|Chemistry|2009|14||0|0:
Set out the ICE table for 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃.
Initially: SO₂ = 5 mol, O₂ = 5 mol, SO₃ = 0.
60% of the SO₂ reacts:
SO₂ used = 0.60 × 5 = 3 mol
By the stoichiometry, O₂ used is half of that:
O₂ used = 3/2 = 1.5 mol
SO₃ formed = 3 mol
At equilibrium:
SO₂ = 5 − 3 = 2 mol
O₂ = 5 − 1.5 = 3.5 mol
SO₃ = 3 mol
total = 2 + 3.5 + 3 = 8.5 mol
Partial pressure is the mole fraction times the total pressure, and the total is 1 atm:
p(O₂) = (3.5/8.5) × 1 = 0.41 atm
Note the total moles fall from 10 to 8.5, since the reaction consumes three moles of gas for
every two produced.
∴ 0.41 atm.
